A rubber band is initially 1 km long. An ant starts walking from one end at a constant speed of 1 cm/s. After each second, the entire band is instantly and uniformly stretched by an extra 1 km (so the ant's position stretches proportionally too, along with everything else). Does the ant ever reach the far end?
choices: It depends on the ant's exact starting speed relative to 1 km/s
Yes — the ant eventually reaches the end, despite the band's length growing without bound
No — the band grows faster than the ant can ever walk, so it never reaches the end
The ant reaches the end only if the growth rate eventually slows down

questions.q: A golfer has an outstanding, career-best round one day, far above their usual average. Ignoring any genuine change in skill, what should you expect, on average, from their very next round?
choices: A round closer to their long-term average than the career-best was
Exactly the same score as the career-best round
An even better round than the career-best
An equally extreme career-best round again

questions.q: You have 12 coins identical in appearance, but exactly one is counterfeit and differs in weight (you don't know if it's heavier or lighter) from the other 11. Using only a balance scale with no weights, what is the minimum number of weighings needed to guarantee identifying the counterfeit AND whether it's heavier or lighter?

During WWII, researchers studied returning bomber planes and found bullet holes clustered on the wings and tail, with very few holes near the engines. Statistician Abraham Wald concluded the military should add armor to the area with the FEWEST bullet holes — the engines. Why?
choices: Because more holes in an area simply means that area already has enough natural armor
Because planes hit in the engine areas were the ones that didn't return, so the lack of holes there reflects fatal damage, not safety
Because bullet holes in the wings indicate structural weakness that needs less reinforcement
Because the enemy specifically avoided targeting the engines, so they needed less protection

questions.q: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test for it is 99% accurate (correctly identifies 99% of those with the disease, and correctly clears 99% of those without it). If a random person tests positive, what is the approximate probability they actually have the disease?

A man lives on the 10th floor. Every morning he takes the elevator to the ground floor. Every evening he rides back up but only to the 7th floor, walking the rest — except on rainy days, when he rides all the way to the 10th floor. Why?
choices: He enjoys the exercise except when it rains
The elevator breaks down above the 7th floor when it's dry
He visits a friend on the 7th floor every dry evening
He is too short to reach the 10th-floor button, but can reach it with his umbrella

questions.q: A family has exactly two children. You are told that the elder child is a girl. What is the probability that both children are girls?
A man buys a horse for $60, sells it for $70, buys it back for $80, then sells it again for $90. How much profit did he make overall?

A puzzle shows people the triple 2, 4, 6 and says it fits a secret rule; they must guess the rule by proposing their own triples and being told 'fits' or 'doesn't fit'. Most participants guess 'ascending even numbers, each +2' and only ever test triples that fit their own guess (like 8, 10, 12), rarely proposing a triple designed to fail — even though the real rule is simply 'any three ascending numbers.' What cognitive bias does this classic experiment, devised by Peter Wason, demonstrate?

You're colouring a map so that no two regions sharing a border have the same colour. According to the Four Colour Theorem, what is the minimum number of colours that is always enough for ANY such map, no matter how many regions it has or how they're arranged?
choices: There is no fixed number — it grows with the number of regions
